general.title_original: Wat Phra Mahathat: 1,500 years of heritage
general.summary_original:
NAKHON SI THAMMARAT — Standing at the heart of Nakhon Si Thammarat for more than 1,500 years, Wat Phra Mahathat Woramahawihan represents more than a place of worship. It is a living record of religious exchange, maritime connections and cultural traditions that shaped Southeast Asia.

The temple was recently recognized as Thailand’s ninth UNESCO World Heritage site and the first in the southern region, marking international recognition of its outstanding cultural significance.

Located on the Malay Peninsula, between the Indian and Pacific oceans, Wat Phra Mahathat developed in an area once connected by major maritime trade routes. These networks brought not only goods and merchants, but also religious beliefs, artistic styles and architectural influences from across Asia.

Over centuries, the temple absorbed influences from Brahmanism, Hinduism, Mahayana Buddhism and Theravada Buddhism, with cultural connections stretching from northeastern India and Sri Lanka to central Java and Mon communities in southern Myanmar.

These diverse influences were transformed into a unique architectural and spiritual identity that later spread throughout Thailand and other parts of Southeast Asia.

At the center of the temple stands the Phra Borom That Chedi, a towering stupa believed by devotees to enshrine relics of the Buddha. According to local tradition, the site was originally an ancient sand dune known as “Hat Sai Kaeo,” where Buddhist relics were discovered before a major religious monument was built there.

Beyond its architecture, UNESCO recognized the temple as a living cultural site where traditions continue to be practiced today.

Among them is the annual Hae Pha Khuen That festival, where devotees bring long pieces of cloth to wrap around the stupa as an act of devotion. The temple is also connected to Nora, a traditional performing art form from southern Thailand that reflects centuries of local beliefs and storytelling.

The recognition of Wat Phra Mahathat is not only about preserving an ancient monument, but also protecting the living heritage surrounding it — including rituals, local knowledge and cultural practices passed down through generations.

The journey toward World Heritage status began in 2009 and took 17 years of preparation, reflecting the temple’s importance not only to Nakhon Si Thammarat, but also to the wider history of Southeast Asia.

Today, Wat Phra Mahathat Woramahawihan stands as a symbol of how cultures, religions and communities have connected across the region for centuries.

general.title_original: Aung San Suu Kyi’s son urges world to demand proof of her safety
general.summary_original:
BANGKOK — Kim Aris, the son of Myanmar’s detained former leader Aung San Suu Kyi, has urged the international community to demand evidence of his mother’s condition and avoid actions that could legitimize Myanmar’s military government.

Speaking in an interview with Radio Free Asia (RFA), Aris criticized reports suggesting that his mother had been moved from prison to house arrest, saying authorities had provided no proof of the claim.

“Half of the international community have been under the wrong idea for the last five years. They have thought that she’s been under house arrest. Actually, she’s been in prison all of this time,” Aris told RFA.

He said Myanmar’s military had repeatedly spread claims about changes to Suu Kyi’s detention status, while the international community accepted the statements without verification.

Aris called on world leaders to follow the example of French President Emmanuel Macron by publicly demanding proof that his mother is alive and calling for the restoration of her basic rights.

“All I can ask for is that the international community and the world leaders follow President Macron of France’s example and make their position very clear and call out for proof that my mother is alive and for her to have her basic human rights restored,” he said.

Suu Kyi, 80, has been detained since Myanmar’s military seized power in a February 2021 coup that removed her elected government. She has been convicted on multiple charges brought by the military authorities, which her supporters and international observers have described as politically motivated.

Aris said the charges against his mother were false and called for her immediate release.

“She’s been sentenced to however many years it is, I don’t know, 25 or 30 years in prison and these charges against her are completely false. In the first place, she should never have been in prison,” he told RFA.

His remarks come as regional efforts continue over how to engage with Myanmar’s military government, with critics warning that greater diplomatic recognition could undermine calls for accountability and human rights.

general.title_original: Police remind public of 48-hour alcohol sales ban
general.summary_original:
BANGKOK — Thai police have reminded businesses nationwide that the sale of alcoholic beverages will be prohibited for 48 hours during Asalha Bucha Day and Buddhist Lent Day, with violators facing up to six months in jail, a fine of up to 10,000 baht, or both.

The Royal Thai Police announced the reminder on Monday as authorities prepare for the upcoming long holiday period, which includes the King’s Birthday on 28 July, Asalha Bucha Day on 29 July and Buddhist Lent Day on 30 July.

National police spokesperson Lt. Gen. Trairong Phiwphan said Police Chief Gen. Kitrat Phanphet has instructed all police units nationwide to step up crime prevention measures and road safety operations during the extended holiday.

Under the ban, the wholesale and retail sale of all alcoholic beverages will be prohibited for 48 hours, from 00:01 on 29 July until midnight on 30 July.

The restriction applies to convenience stores, supermarkets, restaurants selling alcohol, entertainment venues and other retailers, except for locations exempted by law.

The exempted venues include:

  • International airport passenger terminals serving international flights.
  • Licensed entertainment venues operating under Thailand’s Entertainment Places Act.
  • Entertainment-style establishments located in designated tourist zones approved by the Public Health Ministry.
  • Hotels licensed under the Hotel Act.
  • Venues hosting major national or international events designated by the Public Health Ministry.

Police warned that anyone found violating the Alcoholic Beverage Control Act faces a maximum penalty of six months’ imprisonment, a fine of up to 10,000 baht, or both.

Authorities also said police have integrated crime prevention and traffic safety plans to reduce road accidents during the long holiday period.

general.title_original: Thai FM orders probe into Chinese fan incident
general.summary_original:
BANGKOK — Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow has ordered a fact-finding investigation after the Chinese Embassy in Bangkok called on Thai authorities to examine an incident in which a Chinese national was allegedly subjected to excessive force by a security guard at a book event.

Speaking on Tuesday, Sihasak said authorities would first establish the facts before taking any further action.

“We have ordered an investigation to determine exactly what happened. Incidents like this can occur,” he said.

His remarks came a day after the Chinese Embassy urged Thai authorities to promptly investigate the case, which stemmed from an altercation at the International Novel Festival 2026 in Bangkok.

When asked about the large number of Thai social media users criticizing the Chinese Embassy’s Facebook page following its statement, Sihasak said the embassy had the right to issue a public explanation.

“We understand people’s feelings, but it is better to establish the facts and ensure fairness for all parties,” he said.

Asked whether Thailand would coordinate with the Chinese Embassy over the matter, Sihasak said discussions should wait until the investigation is complete.

“Let’s establish the facts first. Once the investigation is finished, we can discuss the matter. We must ensure fairness for all sides,” he said.

The controversy stems from an altercation during the International Novel Festival 2026, where a Chinese attendee was forcibly removed from a reserved seating area by an event security staff member. The incident sparked heated debate online in Thailand and China.

Organizer GMMTV later acknowledged that excessive force had been used by an outsourced security worker, apologized for the incident, and suspended the staff member pending the outcome of an investigation. The company also denied online claims that it had filed legal action against the Chinese attendee.
